description: We are two secondary school teachers from Uruguay specializing in Astronomy, Physics, and Computer Science. We combine space science and open-source web development to turn complex NASA datasets into accessible, interactive, and explorable digital tools. SeleneSight is an interactive platform that simplifies mission planning for the lunar south pole. It enables engineers, educators, and the general public to instantly evaluate and compare Sun and Earth visibility at candidate landing sites.
summary:
SeleneSight is a free, accessible web app for evaluating landing and base sites at the Moon’s south pole. There, the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon, so a hill a few meters high can decide whether a site has power, contact with Earth and how long its night lasts.
Using NASA’s LOLA topography, SeleneSight computes the true horizon of every point between 80° South and the pole. From that horizon it shows sunlight, Earth visibility, the longest night and the longest communication blackout over a full 18.6-year cycle. Sun and Earth positions were validated against JPL Horizons. Users can compare sites, check the nine Artemis III regions, find landing windows for 2027–2030, and see the eclipses that darken the region. They can also have the app suggest power, antenna, habitat and ice-extraction sites linked by the shortest network, with relay antennas where Earth is hidden.
This matters because power, communication and water rarely share one spot, and choosing well reduces risk and cost. SeleneSight meets WCAG 2.2 AA and includes an outreach landing page with articles and activities for students and the public.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

SeleneSight works in two stages. The heavy science runs ahead of time, so the browser only has to look up results and display them.

  • Offline computation (Python):
    • Horizons: for each point we cast 720 horizon rays, one every 0.5°, out to 400 km. The rays include the Moon's curvature and assume an observer 2 m above the ground.
    • Sun and Earth: we track their hourly positions over 18.6 years in the lunar body-fixed frame, with libration included.
    • Visibility: we treat the Sun as a disk and record what fraction of it is visible, because panels gain power gradually as it rises. For Earth we use its centre, because a radio link is either in view or not.
  • Grid: results are stored on a hexagonal grid of 10, 5 and 2 km cells. In the places that matter most, the grid is refined to 40 m: the 38 zones with the shortest nights, the nine Artemis III regions, and the IM-1 and IM-2 sites.
  • In the browser (JavaScript and WebGL): the app reads compact binary files and draws the polar map, the 3D terrain and the sky view. The heavier horizon files load only when a site needs them.

We chose this split deliberately. Precomputing makes every click instant, keeps the app free of any server, and lets the app work offline in a classroom or a field station.

What benefits does it have?

  • Mission-relevant measures, not just averages. A site that is sunny 85% of the time can still have a 26-day night. Battery mass depends on the longest continuous night, so that is the layer we put first. For the same reason we report the longest communication blackout, not just Earth's average visibility.
  • Honest margins. Two sliders add a safety margin for solar and radio shadow. They reflect the uncertainty in the terrain data instead of hiding it.
  • Decisions, not only data. The suggester proposes power, antenna, habitat and ice sites, linked by a minimum spanning tree, with the slopes measured along every link. The communications tool searches for relay paths whose line of sight has been checked against the terrain.
  • Transparency. Every map value is also given as text, and every simplification is listed in the app: centre-of-hexagon values, a ±1 hour time step and a fixed observer height.

What is the intended impact?

For mission planners and students, SeleneSight shows that site selection at the pole is a trade-off between power, communications and water, and that the answer changes with the timescale.

The communications analysis led to a concrete proposal. Malapert Massif has points that never lose sight of Earth, but the Moon's curvature blocks direct line of sight from Shackleton, about 130 km away. With 30 m relay masts, the app finds at least two paths, and that terrain-based chain can back up relay satellites such as ESA's Moonlight.

For the public, the landing page and its activities turn the same data into science outreach in two languages(english and spanish). The app needs no data from students, so teachers can use it in class right away.

What tools did we use?

  • Languages: Python for the data pipeline and JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS for the app.
  • Scientific libraries: NumPy and Numba for the horizon computations, Pillow for the relief image, and Astronomy Engine for the ephemerides.
  • Validation and testing: Sun and Earth positions were checked against NASA/JPL Horizons. Playwright and axe-core ran the automated and accessibility tests.
  • App: three.js (WebGL) for the 3D terrain, a service worker for offline use, and PDFs generated on the device for the quiz certificate.
  • Data: NASA LOLA polar elevation models at 40 m and 240 m, and the USGS outlines of the Artemis III regions.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Claude Code) and Gemini, declared in the visible text, the metadata and the README.
  • Hardware: a standard computer. No special hardware was needed, and the app runs on ordinary phones and laptops.

How is the project creative?

  • The horizon as the starting point. Every result comes from one computed object, the real 360° horizon of each point, which the user can see directly in the sky panel.
  • Guided entry. Explore mode opens with four short stories: the shortest night at Shackleton, the 2029 eclipse, long-term light and Malapert's permanent view of Earth. Plan mode removes the guidance for expert work.
  • Communications as a network problem. Instead of asking only whether a site can see Earth, the app asks how to reach Earth from that site. The network of the four base sites is also solved as a graph problem, a minimum spanning tree, because fewer kilometres of cable and road mean less to launch and less to repair.
  • Learning through play. The word search changes on every visit, and the quiz certificate is drawn with the real horizon of the best point at Shackleton.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific honesty:
    • Results were validated against JPL Horizons.
    • Limitations are stated openly.
    • The 3D view opens at true vertical scale (1×). Exaggerating the relief by default would mislead users about how flat the polar terrain really is, so 2× and 4× are opt-in.
    • Keyboard navigation with visible focus.
    • 44 px touch targets and contrast checked for both text and graphics.
    • Text alternatives for the map and sky charts.
    • Respect for the reduced-motion preference.
    • Bilingual throughout, with English as the default for an international jury.
    • Clear wording and a glossary for non-experts.
    • Vertical, sun-tracking panels, because the Sun stays near the horizon at the pole.
    • Slope limits for the habitat and its routes.
    • Eclipses that darken the whole region at once, which no choice of site can avoid.
    • Landing windows that change if a launch slips.
